utterances.text: I'd like to move on down from that writing to three little pieces of writing in the middle to the left. Can you is he where it says, "Me," "My line," and "Next group"?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you write that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That was written by Ms. Castro, was it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Probably? She wrote "Me," did she?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember who wrote it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Do you think you might have written "Me," and "My line"? I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... because we saw the same letters on another document and I think the question is legitimate, and I wouldn't like any interruptions with him. Now, let me try with -- without trying to interrupt you, Mr. Haynes. You have on that diagram there the words "Next group," and an arrow pointing left. On top -- and then further to the left you have a series of vertical lines. Now, on top of all that you have the words "My line," again, an arrow pointing left with a series of vertical lines. And Mr. Haynes' first question was: Look at those words "My line," "Next group." Did you write those words or was it someone else? Let's start with the words first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't write this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Did you write the arrow? Do you remember putting the arrow yourself, or the two arrows, or either of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I put down the arrows indicating the execution site of my group, where I was lying. So the vertical lines are here to represent where we were and where we were shot. This was the area where I was lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you put those vertical lines on the sketch yourself, on the diagram yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. I don't think I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On -- on the right-hand side of the first set of vertical lines and near that arrow that points to them, there is a horizontal mark pointing to the letters "M-e," and the first question, did you write those letters "M-e"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't remember if it was me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that mark pointing -- the horizontal mark pointing to those two letters, do you remember putting that mark yourself on the sketch or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only drew the lines indicating how we were positioned during the execution. I can't remember writing anything else down when it comes to letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to leave him, give him back to you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to leave that matter there. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There's just one more thing, Mr. Oric. And with respect, Your Honour, and out of an abundance of caution, we better go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we do so, let me ask him one final question. Again, looking at those two letters, do they appear to you to be "M-e" or "M-o"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it looks -- it appears as "M-e" to me. There was a similar case in front of the Bratunac school, so I may have made a mistake. Maybe it was me who wrote it down or somebody else. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I asked you, in fact. Yes, he's back in your hands, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I did ask that we briefly go into private session to conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Is there re-examination, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have questions? I don't have any either. So, Mr. Oric, your testimony finishes here. You will now be assisted by our staff, and arrangements will be made for your return home. On behalf of Judge Kwon, Judge Prost, and Judge Stole and on my own behalf, I would like to thank you for having come over to give testimony, and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, we have had several documents made use of or put to the witness, none tendered so far, so let's start with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At this time the Prosecution would tender document ID 0216-4884. That is a video still. Secondly, a black and white map marked by the witness. If Your Honour please, I can read the items or if we want to move seriatim and rule on them as I state them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have the whole list first and then we'll ask the Defence whether they have any objections. Which is the first one now after the video still?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It is a black and white map marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Which was appended to his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The third item is map 6 from the map book which was also marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Fourth item is the hand-drawn sketch by the witness of Bratunac town, 65 ter number 2094. The fifth exhibit is the same hand-drawn sketch except it's the version that was marked by the witness on the computer screen. The next item is the hand-drawn sketch by the witness of the two digging machines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One doesn't dig, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Your Honour. The excavator and the loader. 65 ter number 2093. The last item is map 5 from the map book, which was also marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Are there any objections from any of the Defence teams regarding the admission of any of these documents? Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would object to the admission of 2094 because this is a sketch that was shown to the witness and depicts the area in front of the school in Bratunac. It remains unclear because there is the word MO or ME for the place where the witness was supposed to be, but at the very moment it is not clear who has put the writings onto the sketch, whether it was the witness or somebody else. This remains unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Anybody else wishes to join that objection? Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Beara would also join in that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I -- for a moment I saw also Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we would like to join Mrs. Nikolic's words, but I would like to add to that one more reason, and that is that somebody else put the writings in that document and indicated the place where that person that was killed was actually killed, which the witness never stated. The witness never pointed to the place where that person was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, you join?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll join too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I see no one else. I see no one else. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of principle, we will join too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. There is a principle involved. I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic, for pointing that out. So basically this is the time when our guidelines come into play, the guidelines at that we gave you in the beginning of this trial. So you know what the position is as regards this document, which is temporarily entered into the records and the others. Now, the Defence teams, or some of the Defence teams, also made use of some documents. Is it your intention to tender any of them or just leave it as having been made use of? Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm a little unclear. Are we -- did Your Honours ask about the first document the Prosecution would like to have admitted into evidence or objections on any of the documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The one that has been objected to is not the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. I was confused. We have an objection to 3, the map prior to the markings, and 7, the map 5 from the map book after the witness had marked on it for the reason that those -- that map contains evidence on it, we believe evidence, and that would be the red markings placed by the Prosecution which go to allegedly stating the execution sites, various execution sites. This witness didn't testify about those. It shouldn't be in evidence. We were going to object when the maps first came out and were brought forward, but we're doing it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness -- it was never put to the witness that the red marks on the map represent anything. I mean, no one suggested that this map was being made use of to indicate the execution sites. It was to explain the route taken from Bratunac up to Konjevic Polje and then turning north rather than turning south, and he was asked to follow the various towns and villages, and I stopped him. I said we can see them, and then we can enter them for the record. The question of markings -- for that matter, there is also marked the boundaries of the enclave there and various other letters which I don't know what they represent, but the witness did not deal with that. So the fact that on that map there are red circles doesn't mean anything for the time being at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that and I understand that. However, if you admit those maps and it becomes evidence we assume you'll rely on that evidence. The red marks denote what the Prosecution believes to be execution sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even so, I don't know where -- we are talking of a map that was used with the witness for the sole purpose of indicating the route taken. I know you say it's route. Indicating the route taken. That was the only purpose of the use of this map, nothing else. I mean, if you still want to object to it, of course you have every right to object to it. I mean, the purpose of my intervention is not to stop you from objecting, but maybe to explain that your objections is without foundation. Maybe, we're not deciding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I appreciate that only if you rely on the direction and not what the Prosecution believe to be these alleged killing sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. But let me follow you up, because you mentioned -- let me go back to the transcript. So -- well, actually I understand now, because you started your intervention by stating that you were confused, and then we have an objection to 3. The map prior to the markings, and 7, the map 5 from the map book after the witness had marked it for the reasons that those map contains evidence that -- so where do we stand, because you objected to two maps, it seems. Actually, you said you had objections to three exhibits, but drop everything, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. You made your ruling. I don't drop anything. My point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't made a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We told you specifically -- I was interrupting you and trying to explain something to you, and not in any way trying to stop you from making an objection and not in any way indicating that we were deciding your objections. But we did confirm to you that these documents, once tendered by the Prosecution and accepted, were only going to serve the sole purpose for which they were intended with this witness, namely to explain the route taken by the trucks or the buses, whatever they were, buses from Bratunac to wherever they stopped. That's -- and the red spots there and any other indication on the map with the exception of the road and the names hasn't got any -- any relevance, at least in our mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is fine? In other words, are you standing by your objection or are you withdrawing it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now you've explained your explanation of it, we would withdraw the objection. However, we don't believe it's proper that the Prosecution would put such maps in front of a witness and on these maps have red dots on the bottom of it which say "Denoting execution sites." If that has not yet been proven and it assumes facts not in evidence at this point, and that's my objection. But you've clarified that, and I trust you as professional Judges will just use these maps for the direction, the route that the witness went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, yes, yes. Yes. Any -- if you want to maintain your objection, we will have it in the record, Mr. Meek, and I will not argue with you any further. Any further objections? No. Mr. Thayer, I saw you standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes just two quick point. Mr. Meek had mentioned the video. I don't know whether that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. We are coming to the Defence Exhibits now, if there are any.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I thought he had an objection to our video. I apologise. The second item, Your Honour, we have just based on the examination of Mr. Haynes been able to obtain the original of the sketch that he finished up with the witness showing. We have the actual original. We have always been using photocopies, it's just been our practice, but we actually do have the original. I can offer it up to the Court just to assist the Court in its examination of the evidence. We had not intended to use this. It wasn't on our exhibit list, but we do have the actual original. It was created in 1995 during the interview. I just offer that as assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's -- it's at the end of the statement. I mean, one could see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It is the sketch of the -- of the killing site, the execution site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- no, but you did not put any questions to the witness on that so leave it at this point in time. You had the option -- so, now, any of the Defence teams would like to tender any documents as exhibits? Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. The Defence would like to tender for admission document number 3D7, page 1 of the statement given between 10 and 12 August, 1995, given by this witness and signed by him, as well as the 11th page of that same statement, as well as the clean version of document 2094, Exhibit number 65 ter 2094, because we would like to contest some of the evidence given by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this the same document, same drawing?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The same drawing but without the markings that the witness made in the courtroom. Without the red arrows that were put subsequently on the witness's direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not already tendered by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand the situation well, I believe that the only thing that was tendered was the version with the witness's markings. I may be wrong --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My understanding is both are tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number 4 and number 5 as you have named it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, very well. I thank you. In that case, just the statement pages 1 and 11 of document 3D7. That's the only thing we would like to tender, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Any further -- yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We got six documents that we would like to tender into evidence, and I will go in order that they were used by Mr. Stojanovic during his cross-examination. The first document was article in the newspaper Slobodna Dalmacija containing interview with the witness. It is Defence number 4D/7, with English translation. Second is part of video with number V000/4417. And the relevant part of this video is already provided to Madam Registrar, and it has number 4D4/14. I believe we were informed, actually, that a surrogate sheet for this sheet will appear on e-court, but we provided the registry with a copy of this video. Third document that we would like to tender into evidence is document of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina General Staff. It's interim report dated July 13, 1995. It has Defence number 4D-13. We were informed by the translators that we will receive today English translation of this document. So far we checked a minute ago, but it still hasn't appeared. Fourth document that we would like to tender into evidence is -- is opening address by army commander of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Rasim Delic, before the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly and it's titled "Fall of Srebrenica," and dated 13th of July, 1996. It bears Defence number 4D-5, and it has English translation. Next document is a statement of Ramiz Becirevic. It's dated August 11, 1995. Defence number 4D-2, with English translation. And the sixth document that we would like to tender is interim report by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina General Staff, dated August 4, 1995. Defence number 4D-10. And we are still waiting for translation. We are informed that it will be tendered today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I notice Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Chairman. The document 3 about Bosnia and Herzegovina concerning Ramiz Becirevic, and document 525 - -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment. I can't follow you like this. Document 3? Which documents 3 about Bosnia-Herzegovina concerning Ramiz Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's document 5D3 in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. This is not the same one that has been -- or has been tendered by Mr. Lazarevic, is it? Is it the statement of Ramiz Becirevic of 11 August, 1995? It's a different one. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. It's the document by the army of the Republic of Bosnia Herzegovina of June 30, 1995. Then document 5D5, which is a video clip together with a transcript of that video. And then document 5D7, which is the document from the Chief of Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina of 7 February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Any further documents that you wish to tender? None? Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just informed that English translation of document 4D-13 has just arrived and it will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said you were going to receive it today. Mr. Thayer. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Taking the suggestion of Judge Kwon, in future -- now, we try to adopt this because we are a crowd in here, so we try to do it this way: In preparation of this stage, which will happen at the end of each testimony, please prepare on a piece of paper the documents that you wish to tender, in other words, that they will be -- they will be provided to the Prosecution. You can even provide them as you go along so that the Prosecution will then be ready on their feet to say no objection or object. Are their any objections on the part of the Prosecution to any of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The -- there is no objection to any of the documents even though only portions were either played or shown. We have no objection to them coming in in their entirety. I would note, though, with respect -- I believe it was to the last document to which Madam Fauveau referred, the February 7th document, I believe it was the testimony of the witness that he had absolutely -- that's 5D7, Your Honour, he want familiar with it, had never seen it before, and I would therefore object that there's been no foundation laid for it or there's no relevance to the document. He was not able to authenticate it in any fashion. But other than that, Your Honour, no objections at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you know the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the fact a document may not be confirmed by a witness does not render it inadmissible ab initio or a priori. So we have to say that. But if you wish to register an objection, please do so by all means and it will enter into the records and it will be considered in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position is that the witness has not given you any comfort, Madam Fauveau, in relation to this document. For the time, rather than being definitively admitted, it's being marked for identification along the lines indicated in our guidelines. And then of course you can seek to have it confirmed by another witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour. Given the hour of the day, and I understand from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have still got a lot of work to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I understood, Your Honour. I have a witness concern in mind. I understand from Mr. Haynes that he estimates perhaps 20 minutes of oral argument, and given that it may -- may take some time, I was wondering if the Court was in a position to permit us to let the witness go for the day. It seems that it may take a fair amount of time on the issue. I just wanted to raise that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think you can -- you can do that, and that will give us sufficient time to deal with this outstanding motion as thoroughly as upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. However, listen, I want to make sure that either Victims and Witnesses Unit explain to him and apologise to him, or else if they find it uncomfortable, please get the witness in here and I'll do it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't like a witness staying here one whole afternoon here and being sent home without explaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We share that view, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want a confirmation that will be done or has been done. Thank you. So the rest of the documents are admitted, of course. Now, we -- we come to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm behind the pillar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise to you, but I can do nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I can see you or Judge Kwon but not both from back here. I did put two pages of a document to Mr. Oric, they're 7D3 and the pages reference numbers are 38 and 75. So that's 7D-38 and 7D-75. That's the English part of his statement of the 12th of August, 1995, and the drawing of the site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. They are so admitted and marked accordingly. Sorry, I apologise to the interpreters. I shouldn't bang.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is the same witness statement used by another Defence -- but pages are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The only page technically, Judge Kwon, that needs to go in is the drawing, which is page 55. I'm not going to ask that the front page of a witness statement that simply bears his signature goes in on behalf of two or three defendants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That obviously makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's the page where the diagram is, 3D7, not 7D3 -- all right. I stand corrected. It's not 7D3 or it's 3D -- all right. Okay. Leave it then. You would make the adjustment. So as I suggested yesterday, considering the urgency of the matter because of the proximity of the arrival of Witness Ruez, the oral submissions in the wake of the Defence motion that I referred to yesterday which was filed yesterday will be heard today. Now, on the part of the Defence, do you have one combined submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I take it and how long do you wish to - -

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I will abide by any restriction you wish to place on me. I can do it in five, 10, or 15 minutes. I'm not going to unnecessarily repeat that which you have already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you should, and this is why I'm asking you how much time you require. Or do you wish to hear what the Prosecution position is?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I had anticipated that would be the way to do it because everything we have to say is in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the way I had anticipated too but then I heard Mr. McCloskey say that you wished to address us for 20 minutes or so, so I thought there was an agreement between you already and how you were to proceed. All right. So let's hear Mr. McCloskey first. We should have a break now? I see. All right. Oh, yes, yes, yes. I've been working since 9.00 this morning nonstop, so 20 minutes here and 30 minutes there. Judge Kwon has been working with me since 9.00 this morning. So let's have a break of 30 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's do it this way: Mr. McCloskey will respond orally to the Defence motion. Of course, the Defence will then have an opportunity to make submissions arising out of the response, but also in pursuant to what you requested in the motion itself. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, it's all yours. How long do you anticipate? Five minutes? Two? One?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Two to three hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think your first estimate is hopefully the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Take your time. I don't think it requires much more than that from either side, before you course if you need more than that we will give you. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was my first point. One of the reasons that I felt comfortable in responding to a 20-page motion on one day's notice orally was because I'm not really sure we have a big issue here. The Prosecution certainly objects to any prior ruling regarding Mr. Ruez's testimony, because we really haven't reached a point where any issues have ripened themselves to -- to cause the necessary ruling. It appears to me that the -- the Defence -- the foundation of the Defence's concerns are based on the prior testimony of Mr. Ruez in the Krstic case and in the Blagojevic case. The Prosecution, as you know or will so soon, are not offering the transcripts or the evidence of Mr. Ruez in the Krstic case nor the Blagojevic case, and we're not offering in detailed report analysing 1.800 witnesses or witness statements or, as we see from the Milosevic case, Judge Kwon mentioned -- I think he was quoting

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "An overall analysis and overview of the effect of the evidence." I hope you got that in my opening statement and I hope you get that in my closing statement. You will hear some analysis of the evidence in that context, I hope, from Mr. Butler, but that is not point of Mr. Ruez's testimony. And let me just tell you a few things that we won't be doing. I'm not going to ask Mr. Ruez to speculate. I'm not going to be asking him to go into long narratives, and if he perhaps slips into a narrative I will stop him, and I'm sure the Court will. Nor will I ask him to make inappropriate conclusions that will not be helpful for the Court. And I will make every effort to follow the law as it's been set down in this Chamber. Now, having said that, I want to just briefly go to the Krstic and Blagojevic cases. I know they're not on trial here, but Mr. Ruez, with Judge Rodrigues and his experience here and background from Portugal led a very, very different case than other cases and preferred that the lawyers be kept to a minimum and that the witness be allowed to expand, and in that Chamber they encouraged Mr. Ruez to speak and they wanted his views and they wanted his advice, and so he was encouraged to go on and on, and that's not necessary. We know the Trial Chamber we're in front of. As you know, Mr. Nicholls knows you very well, and we have seen in the last three witnesses what to expect. We realise we're not in the Krstic Chamber any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he does know me very well, I'm surprised that he chose to appear before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if you want me to tell you what he said I will, but maybe we'll leave that out. And in the Blagojevic Chamber, it was similar. Judge Liu and the panel allowed Mr. Ruez to provide explanations, and they sought him out, and Mr. Ruez is a talkative Frenchman, and very involved in this case, and in that environment he will speak his mind and he will talk. That's -- that's not my particular style. And while I was the lead counsel in the Blagojevic case, I did not lead Mr. Ruez, but we led it in the context of that Trial Chamber. We're getting to know this Trial Chamber. It is not our intention to get into the problems that I understand counsel are concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I stop you here and maybe you can address this issue. It has been put to you that the number of hours you are anticipating Mr. Ruez will be testifying in direct in this trial basically even exceed the amount of hours that he took when he testified in either Blagojevic or in Krstic, and the question, therefore, arises if you're going to ask him to speculate, if you're not going to give him the rope and let him say what he wants to say and you're not going to put any inappropriate -- ask him or let him reach any inappropriate conclusions and you're following the law, how come he's going to -- or you anticipate 15 hours and from what we have seen so far, 15 hours become easily 20 here if not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that estimate included the cross- examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not what the Defence submitted. The Defence submitted that the estimate of 15 hours was exclusive of cross- examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I hope that it won't take as long as it might, but given the fact that this is such a big case and that there are so many accused and that we just were abundantly, you know, conservative on that point. Mr. Ruez has identified some 260 photographs that -- of some 24 crime scenes and certain maps, and it's our intention that he go over each of the crime scenes and talk about them and what he saw and what he observed and -- and this may be the key bone of contention, Mr. Ruez will also be asked to provide information on the context of why he goes, for example, to the Kravica warehouse. And so he will be providing some hearsay information in order to put the places he's talking about in context. For example, he will -- one of his first documents is a photograph of Potocari, and he will identify the various factories and buildings that are relevant to your review of Potocari where he learned, from the investigation, Muslims were staying. He's not going to make any other conclusions, I hope, about that, but you'll need to hear that the reasons these are important is these were the places he heard about that people were staying. The same thing with the white house, this famous white house you've already seen a photograph of with the people standing on the balcony. He will show you where that white house is. That will help you sort it out both when the Dutch start speaking of it and when you go there. He may say -- he will say he received information from the Muslims or from the witness, Mr. Kingori, that people were at the white house. Then we'll show a picture of the men standing at the white house. So there will inevitably, as there is with any homicide investigator who goes to a crime scene, you know, talk about what he learned in his investigation to put it in overall context, and that is the way I intend to lead Mr. Ruez. And I don't intend to have him go into a summary of the case. He's -- in the last two cases, he was our first witness, and so we did always ask him to provide a bit of the summary, the two fundamental issues, the column goes one way, the public goes the other, and just to give a little background. Well, this time, as you've seen, we have chosen to start with the victims who have done that. And while Mr. Ruez might have a map that just points in the two directions, that's purely as an exhibit to help you remember that, and I don't -- I'm not going to have him go into a long discussion of a column and where these people went and where that people went. I'm going to limit it to these -- these sites and why things are relevant. This will include, "How did you find out about a particular crime scene?" And he'll be able to say, "I received information, A, B and C. We went and checked it out. We found this, and here are the pictures of what we found." And I think the information that he will give that is hearsay will help you understand the actual evidence better. If you remember from their motion, I think they're concerned with his prior testimony. They have never suggested that his photos or his exhibits of the prior testimony or the current ones aren't relevant and appropriate. That's his evidence. They're not -- what we would like you to review is the context by which it comes in and under the rules of this Tribunal, that hearsay can be viewed as evidence. You can give it whatever weight you'd like. In some systems we'd instruct the jury that you may take this evidence not for the truth of the matter asserted but for the reasons he acted or state of mind or something else. As you know, we don't need to do that here. We're not trying to protect a jury. It's really up to you to give it whatever weight you want to put to it. If you look at the judgement in Blagojevic or Krstic you won't see Mr. Ruez citing evidence. You'll see one time that Mr. Ruez -- he knew of Potocari because he'd been there. He looked at a video of General Krstic giving an interview in front of certain buildings, and he was able to say, "I've been there. I've studied this video. General Krstic was standing in X." It's one of the few things where Ruez has cited as evidence. This is normal. This is I don't think will be objectionable to anyone. The same thing with Lieutenant Colonel Popovic. So this is the kind of thing I expect. There will be bumps in the road. There will be periods where I -- I may go off the chart. He may go off the chart. I know you'll catch us or we'll catch ourselves but I don't think there's any need for any ruling. I don't think we have -- we deserve to be ruling -- any ruling at this point. A little guidance might help, though I have a pretty good feel for -- for where you're coming from and we can read Judge Kwon's views on the subject. I largely share them. But -- so just to finish, I don't really think we have a problem, and any guidance you might want to give us is always appreciate. And I think you might find I'm in the asking Mr. Ruez questions you may be interested in, and so I -- you know, if you are, please ask away. There's a -- we have a -- what we call a trial video that takes some two to three hours and it's a compilation of actual video shot at the time and the dates, and it was -- most of this material was accumulated during Mr. Ruez's time frame. So he's here merely to say this is the stuff I picked up. We're going to play that video. The only time I really am asking him to pause it is every once in awhile, we'll see an accused. You'll probably recognise the accused, but they're a little younger. It's a wartime. So we'll have him identify the accused, and we'll pretty much leave it at that unless comes up that I think you really need some help on. The Hotel Fontana footage which takes an hour or two we're not going to play for Mr. Ruez. The Dutch people that were there will see that. So I don't think it will be a problem, and Mr. Ruez is not meant to be here as a linkage person to tie in the various units and the people we see on the film, and so we're not going to get into that with him. So again, I don't think there's a problem. I think we'll get through it like the pros we are, and I think you'll be happy with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Haynes obviously doesn't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's half past 6.00 on the immediate night before Mr. Ruez is about to begin his testimony next Wednesday, and it's probably over 10 years since he began this investigation. It's made plain in the motion, and I want to underline the point now, he has never made a witness statement in this case, and it is our collective experience, both within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal and nationally from wherever we come from, that is a wholly unique event. He is the chief investigator, and we have to wait to be told by Mr. McCloskey until half an hour before he goes into the witness box what he is going to say in evidence. And from what I've just heard from Mr. McCloskey telling us that he's going to give a summary of this and hearsay as to that, we are right to rely on the 430-odd pages of transcript that we've had to read to glean what his evidence is going to be before this Tribunal next Wednesday, because it sounds very much from what Mr. McCloskey says that with a couple of tweaks here and there, it's going to be precisely the same as it has been before. You've not been addressed on one matter of law, and I take it as read, really, that the -- actually, five Trial Chamber authorities and one appellate decision are accepted by the Prosecution to be a correct statement of the law of evidence as the admissibility of evidence from Prosecution investigators. It is quite simply, beyond factual matters, inadmissible. Now, we have thought long and hard about this. It has been our collective view for some time now that what happened in Krstic and Blagojevic could not and should not happen again. And we could have left this till the morning that he arrived to give evidence, as indeed Judge Kwon will know happened on three or four occasions in the Milosevic case. We could have spent day after day, week after week, jumping up and down saying, "That's not a proper question. That's not a proper question," and turned his evidence into a broken, disjointed, unpalatable event, but we decided to go by this route, to ask for a ruling at this juncture, and we believe that is proper. It is courteous to the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber and the witness, and it is wholly appropriate. It's appropriate really, for three reasons. Firstly, because this is a very important decision. Secondly, because it is likely that it is not the last time that you will have to consider this in this case, and we feel it is important that a benchmark is set down now. And thirdly, because of Mr. Ruez himself. I don't know whether uniquely I have studied his evidence in the sort of depth I have. You'll see the summary I have prepared for you at Annex A to the motion and the section that I quoted of his evidence in Blagojevic which really gives the flavour of it. It's story-telling. That's what he does. But the phrase was used during the opening of this case, I think by Mr. Ostojic and Mr. McCloskey, "empty vessel." Mr. Ruez is quite the other end of the scale from an empty vessel. He is a very full vessel. He's got a lot of information and a lot of opinions, and no one can blame him. He's very anxious to give them. He will forgive me. I've actually met him. Mr. McCloskey introduced me to him, but he'll forgive me if I describe him as a warm bottle of champagne. You give him the slightest agitation and the cork flies out and the contents are everywhere. You will have seen in the motion that I drafted for you that in response to one simple question in the Blagojevic case, namely "How far is Bratunac from Potocari," he gave an answer that went on for 25 minutes, and it included his views as to this, that, and the other, his assessment of people he'd spoken to who this Trial Chamber are never going to hear, and the like. It's very kind of Mr. McCloskey to offer to let us all suck it and see, but no thank you. We would like you to rule on the admissibility of Mr. Ruez's evidence in this trial and to do it now. There are a few more points I'd like to make. I'm going to address the professional Judges point, even though I think it's been raised, but I will address it. You are, of course, professional Judges, which means that you have the ability to assess and deal with evidence which you would normally protect a jury or a lay assessor from. You're a bit like parents looking after children, but when you're on your own, you can look after yourself. You will forgive me giving you another little analogy, but it's a bit like dealing with evidence, having fish for dinner. As adults, you can choose whether you fillet it or whether you eat the bones, and that is what you are capable of doing. You're capable of dealing with the bones of the evidence or filleting it. But what the Prosecution want you to do in this case, not as a substitution but as a supplement, is to have a side order of fish fingers. It's food so heavily processed that it's lost all its original flavour, but it comes nicely wrapped with instructions on the packet how to cook it and with some serving suggestions. That's what, in legal terms, we'd call of no probative value and wholly unnecessary. That's the language of the Trial Chamber. I want to address you also about questions of public perception and the rules of natural justice. These are very serious charges and this Tribunal is subject to worldwide scrutiny. While the public do not necessarily have to have legal knowledge, lawyers and Judges have always have to have regard to public perception of their process. I make this submission with the greatest of trepidation, but I mean it with all respect. Mr. Ruez was an employee of the United Nations, as is Mr. McCloskey, and as are you. We all accept and understand the concept of the independence and objectivity of counsel and judiciary. The public, I fear, may not see it that way, and justice has, at the end of the day, to be seen to be done. A conviction based wholly or just in part on evidence of this sort would shock, I fear, the public. Can I move on, please, to discuss something else that was raised by Mr. McCloskey, namely the question of prior practice. Repeated bad practice doesn't make good practice, and this trial is not a rerun of Krstic or Blagojevic. In our submission, counsel and the Trial Chamber got it wrong in Blagojevic. I'm bound to say I have some sympathy for those who defended Krstic, because as I said to you earlier, Mr. Ruez has not, in 11 years, ever made a witness statement. Quite how they were supposed to prepare for his evidence when he walks through the courtroom, the door of the courtroom with his maps and videos, having had no notice whatsoever of what he was about to say, I simply do not know. It's perhaps unsurprising that they raised no objection, but that such a thing could happen in such a serious trial in the 21st century I regard as incredible. Lastly -- last but one, effective trial management. It's early in the trial, but this is a seminal moment, not just in terms of the evidential ruling but in terms of the size and shape of the thing we're trying to deal with. We've had two weeks, and we've had two witnesses, and things are slipping a little bit. It's very difficult to make this submission without it sounding like a threat. That may in part be due to the inadequacy of my advocacy, but if it's going to sound like a threat, I might as well go for it. Open that door to Mr. Ruez and the sort of testimony that we know he's going to give, and you are opening Pandora's box. You will be opening the door to months of summary evidence, conclusive evidence, argumentative evidence, theory, rumour, and speculation. If I may tell you a little story. A few days ago, somebody handed me a book they thought I should read. It was called "Srebrenica, The Unspoken Truth," and it was remarkable but for the bibliography at the back of the text was longer than the text itself. It was absolutely crammed full with the names and details of people who had written articles about Srebrenica. Each of them, probably all of them, have come to different conclusions to Mr. Ruez, and each of them has come across what passes for investigations, and each of them are doubtless as anxious as Mr. Ruez to come and tell you about it. Close the door to Mr. Ruez and his presentation, because that is what it was called in Krstic and Blagojevic, not evidence, a presentation, and you will have this case under control. And moreover, you will know that you have brought it under control by applying the laws of evidence, and what better way is there to get a case under control than that? Far better to do it that way than to have to resort to artificial means of trial management, limiting the time available to parties to present their cases, restricting the time for cross and the like. One principle you won't find me arguing against is that a speedier trial is a fairer trial. My last point is this: The jurisprudence of this Tribunal is settled and consistent. It has been so for three or four years, and the Prosecution have known that. They could at any time since the Milosevic decisions have caused their chief investigator to make a witness statement in this case. We could have read it. We could have said we don't mind him saying this, that, and the other, but we don't want all his conclusions. That would have been placed before you in a proper --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please speak into the microphone. Could counsel please speak into the microphone and repeat the last few sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We still are more than prepared to admit every plan, every map, refer I video, every photograph. What it is. What it shows. That's how it's done in homicide investigations. That's how it was done in Milosevic when the Trial Chamber came to the rulings that it did. The rulings of this Tribunal are not only consistent and monotonous, they are at a piece with the state of law in every jurisdiction that we know about and the contrary view is simply untenable. I have no question that as an investigator, Mr. Ruez's integrity and professionalism are beyond compare and I, for one, would find it fascinating to listen to him and his theories, but not here, not in a criminal trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Haynes, you would not deny that there are some parts which are admissible, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, he can -- he can quite properly say, "I took this photograph. It's a photograph of the Kravica warehouse."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why do we close the door then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Because causing him to come here and say, "I took a photograph," is a waste of his time. We can happily deal with that by written agreed facts. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You haven't covered specifically what you would agree. In your motion, you said you can agree that nothing is offered for the agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We will agree that every exhibit is what it is, shows what it shows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could address this concrete example offered by the -- by Mr. McCloskey. He offered Mr. Ruez can give evidence as to the context, why he went to Kravica warehouse. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I submit that is inadmissible evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Because it involves his summary of other evidence that leaves -- that leaves him upon that inquiry and his conclusion as to why he went there. Can I give you an example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's suppose that he is an extraordinarily resourceful investigator and he went there on a hunch. Is that admissible evidence? Does that have any probative value? It has no more probative value if he says to you, as he will do, "I was told by several survivors that they were arrested near a road by a pylon where there was a railway track nearby, and I embarked upon an investigation to try and find out where -- what they were talking about." You are straight away there into the sort of material that the Trial Chamber in Milosevic, the Appeals Chamber in Milosevic, and the Trial Chamber in Kordic said is inadmissible and non-probative material from an investigator. Placing it into context is just another way of saying, Let him give an explanation. Let him tell his story. And so I do submit that how he came to investigate a particular site is of itself offensive. It's what you should not be hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He's not telling how the killing had happened, but he just tried to give evidence as to the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But he is. The one follows the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just like the map. The map was used to identify the roads in the case of the previous witness, but there was the red point marking --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: With respect, Judge Kwon, the previous witness was a witness of fact. He was in Srebrenica. This is how you prove cases like this. This is how you adduce evidence. You get your witness of fact and you take him to the map. You take him to the video. You say, as we've seen, "Is that the gymnasium where you were held? Is that the road you went down?" That's the way you do it. Hearing Mr. Ruez say, "I have been told by witnesses that this is the road they went down," is precisely the sort of material that is probative of nothing, repetitive of what you've heard everywhere else and which is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but what happens in domestic jurisdictions, any murder case, for example, homicide case? Just take a very simple case of the CID inspector or the main inspector, investigator in a murder that has received information by a person whose name he cannot reveal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly in my jurisdiction you wouldn't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He wouldn't be able to find, locate the weapon used in a murder in such-and-such a place. According to you, the investigator, if summoned to give evidence cannot even say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: He can say he recovered a gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if he is asked -- but if he is asked the we, "How come that you went specifically to that location," you say that question is inadmissible and his would-be answer is also inadmissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, to take that position is to take the position that the law of hearsay, in its strictest, form would apply. And in fact, using your own example, perhaps you can respond to this, the statement by the investigator as to why he went to a particular road would be admissible in countries that apply a strict rule of hearsay on the basis that he's not adducing it for the purpose of the statement but simply to give a context of why he went to a particular point. So it would be admissible in an a contextual sense. You're saying in a Tribunal where hearsay is in fact admissible, that we would apply an even instructor rule than in national jurisdictions where hearsay is applied quite rigidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The difficulty is with that that you can take these simple examples, but this is -- this is really a million miles away from what you get from Mr. Ruez. Mr. Ruez tells a story. You've read the passage in the motion. It is impossible to dissect the sources of information that go into that sort of testimony. You know, for my part, no, I don't suppose I have a particular difficulty if he's going to say, "I went to the Kravica warehouse because most of the information I received indicated it was an execution site." But the difficulty I do have is when he begins to say, as he does very, very often, "We found a site which we believed to be an execution site. We've got no witnesses who say they were executed there, but we looked at this and this made it look like it was an execution site, and then we heard a rumour from some people in Germany that people were killed there, and when we looked back at it --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this point. This is complete nonsense. It has no basis of fact. He's making it up, as far as I can see, and he's misleading the Court. I can go into that very event if you like but this is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to go into that also because we are not aware of that. But I think you've made your point. Any further -- further submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. Is there anything else I can help you with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One thing I want to make sure of. It seems that you both agree with the jurisprudence that we have in this Tribunal. You do not -- you do not contest --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very, very sorry. There is one more decision I discovered which is again in the Milosevic case. It's a decision on the admissibility of Morten Torkildsen's evidence dated the 22nd of March, and it's the fourth consistent decision as to the admissibility on the basis of ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You both stand by that decision? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. President. And if I could have one minute to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This appears to me the first time we've seen this kind of language and the attack personally on Mr. Ruez and on the Honourable Trial Chambers from the two previous cases. It's inappropriate and I don't think it helps the Court. And I think the issues we've talked about, that's not the law in the Old Bailey which you can show a picture, and the presumptions of Mr. Ruez and his presence in French courts and the courts of Europe and the courts of China, these are honourable systems and I -- they're being completely overlooked, not to mention most importantly our system, the ICTY system, which is a combination of both, and I think you understand that, and we will do our best to follow the rules of this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I thank you. I don't think we have -- go ahead Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, I just had one point for clarification based on something you said. Are you advancing the position that we should adopt this what I would call a pre-emptive ruling approach in the case, the specific case of Mr. Ruez, or are you suggesting that this is something that we should be looking at that may be applicable in relation to other witnesses produced by the Prosecution or by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm inviting you to make a pre-emptive ruling in the case of Mr. Ruez. I think it's plain from, I think, the section in the motion that's headed "Procedural matters" that in my view, in my submission, if you do agree that there are limits to what he can properly be examined-in-chief about, that then some time ought to be taken to explain to him what the ruling is so that -- so that he knows. But it is - - it is Mr. Ruez, and I generally didn't mean to be offensive to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If by giving the champagne analogy, I didn't mean to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can give it at that. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One more minute there is a point I missed and -- my handwriting is not so good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One thing very unique to all of us in this place is the scope of these crimes, the 24 incredible crime scenes with thousands and thousands of victims. If we were to stand by a rule as strict as this, would we have to bring back every woman to back up which warehouse she went to and the white house, and each of the areas. Without Mr. Ruez's ability to say why he did something or where he went, we would be forced to call all these people. We would be here until 2020 and that's not what this institution is about, nor what any other court is about. But to think about that when you're thinking of the number of crime scenes, 92 bis, these things are unique to this institution. We need to be able to have hearsay for this very purpose, not to speculate, not to go in areas that don't help you but these are big cases and they need some flexibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we've heard enough. We'll hand down our decision in due course, obviously before Mr. Ruez arrives here. Thank you. Have a nice evening. Yes, we will be sitting again on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.57 p.m.,
